articles.title: Closure Order Issued for Phantom The Lounge Due to Carbon Monoxide Risks
articles.excerpt: Phantom The Lounge in Rochdale has been ordered to close after environmental health officers discovered excessive carbon monoxide levels and breaches of smoke-free regulations.
articles.content_html:
A shisha lounge on Maclure Road, Rochdale, has been handed a closure order due to excessive levels of carbon monoxide (CO) found on site. The order was granted at Manchester Magistrates’ Court on 24 July 2026, following evidence presented by environmental health officers from Rochdale Borough Council, supported by Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service (GMFRS) and Greater Manchester Police (GMP).

Routine inspections revealed that Phantom The Lounge had been illegally operating, with smoking taking place in a substantially enclosed area, violating the Smoke-Free regulations under the Health Act 2006. Officers also identified hazardous practices in the kitchen, which further endangered the health of customers and staff, with CO levels exceeding 100 parts per million (PPM).

On two occasions, GMFRS insisted that customers and staff leave the premises for their safety. Despite the council offering the owners an opportunity to rectify the issues, the business refused to cooperate and continued to operate without making necessary changes, prompting the council to take court action as a last resort.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader and portfolio holder for Climate Change and Environment, stated that the high levels of CO posed a serious risk to health. She commended the environmental health officers and partners for their intervention, which prevented further danger to the public.

articles.title: Rochdale Local Plan Moves Forward with Public Consultation
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Local Plan, outlining housing and transport developments until 2039, has progressed to public consultation following council approval, with nearly 11,000 new homes planned.
articles.content_html:
A council meeting on July 28 approved the borough's Local Plan, which will guide development and housing strategies until 2039. The plan includes the construction of nearly 11,000 new homes and significant changes to local transport stations. Following revisions to a 175-page document, the plan is set to enter public consultation before its expected formal adoption in 2027.

Originally, the plan mandated that new housing developments include 20 per cent affordable housing. However, this requirement has been reduced to 15 per cent due to financial viability concerns. Councillor Daniel Meredith stated that this adjustment does not reflect a diminished commitment to affordable housing, noting that the council has delivered 883 affordable homes in the past five years, exceeding previous targets.

The Local Plan is part of a broader strategy that includes the Places for Everyone plan, which aims to build around 175,000 homes across Greater Manchester over the next two decades. The Rochdale borough is also set to benefit from the Atom Valley scheme, which envisions 7,000 new homes and 20,000 jobs, alongside the development of the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre in Kingsway.

The plan places a strong emphasis on housing and transport, with a focus on reconfiguring land around transport hubs along the Manchester to Leeds railway line. This initiative aims to create vibrant communities around stations in Rochdale, Castleton, Mills Hill, Smithy Bridge, Littleborough, and a new Slattocks station, enhancing local economic growth and community engagement.

articles.title: Neglected toddler admitted to hospital 19 days after social services closed her case
articles.excerpt: A 19-month-old girl, referred to as Child K1, was admitted to hospital in critical condition after social services closed her case, revealing severe neglect and malnutrition.
articles.content_html:
A 19-month-old girl, referred to as Child K1, was admitted to hospital in critical condition 19 days after social services closed her case, according to a Child Safeguarding Practice Review (CSPR) in Rochdale. The report revealed that the toddler was severely neglected, weighing just 9.7lb (4.4kg) at the time of her admission, which is less than half the average weight for her age.

The review, conducted by expert reviewer Nicki Walker-Hall, found that the child was suffering from severe dehydration and had no fatty tissue on her body. She was described as having "paper-thin skin" and was covered in open pressure sores extending along her back, hips and bottom. The case was closed despite previous warnings about a mother, who was just 17 when the child was born, neglecting her daughter.

Concerns about Child K1's welfare were raised multiple times before her hospital admission. A family member had informed hospital staff in April 2024 that the mother was neglecting the child, but social services concluded that the mother was willing to accept support. However, subsequent visits revealed that the basic needs of the child were not being met, and the mother avoided contact with social workers and health visitors.

Following an anonymous tip in December 2024, social workers visited the home and confirmed the child's condition. Despite this, they were unable to secure the mother's consent for further intervention, leading to the case being closed. The review concluded that the child's severe malnutrition and dehydration could have led to death if emergency treatment had not been administered in time.

articles.content_html:

The latest budget forecast, presented at a town hall meeting, indicates that rising wage costs, inflation, and increased pressures in adult social care and children’s services are contributing factors to this financial shortfall.

The finance team highlighted uncertainty regarding future government funding settlements, which complicates budget planning. Budget documents noted a risk that the finance settlement for 2029/30 may not include a continuation of the Recovery Grant, which is currently around £15 million and only confirmed until 2028/29.

In adult social care, the 'real living wage' is increasing at a rate higher than anticipated, further straining budgets. An additional £1.5 million per year has been incorporated into future costs to address these pressures. Overspending in children’s services has also exceeded initial forecasts, a trend that has been observed in recent years, according to finance officer Sam Smith.

Councillor Daniel Meredith stated at the meeting on July 28 that significant efforts are underway to develop new care homes and children’s homes, expressing optimism about addressing the challenges in both children and adult services.
